items.prompt: What is a proxy?
choices: A measurement repeated several times and then averaged to cut noise
A second instrument used to double-check the first one's reading
An observable stand-in believed to move with the real target
A unit that converts one quantity into another kind of quantity
items.explanation: A proxy is something you can observe that is assumed to track something you cannot.

items.prompt: Which of these is a proxy for how much a student has learned?
choices: The student's score on a final exam
The number of desks in the classroom
The student's height in centimeters
The temperature of the classroom today
items.explanation: An exam score is observable and is believed to move with learning. The others have no such link.

items.prompt: Test coverage is used to stand in for something. Which one is the target?
choices: Line coverage
Lines of code
Review count
Code quality
items.explanation: Coverage is the proxy you can read. Code quality is the target nobody can read off directly.

items.prompt: Which addition turns "the app got faster" into an actual measurement?
choices: A stronger adjective, such as noticeably faster for most users
A unit and a baseline, such as p99 in ms before and after
A screenshot of the dashboard pasted into the team chat
The name of the engineer who shipped the change last week
items.explanation: A measurement is checkable. A unit plus a before/after baseline lets someone else verify it.

items.prompt: You weigh yourself, then yourself holding a bag, and subtract. What kind of measurement is that?
choices: Indirect: two observable readings are combined
Direct: the bag was placed on the scale alone
A sample: only a small part of the bag was weighed
A proxy: the scale reports the bag's price
items.explanation: The bag was never weighed alone. Its weight is inferred from two readings you could observe.

items.prompt: Your readings are 70 kg alone and 93 kg holding the suitcase. What is the suitcase's weight?
choices: 93 plus 70, which is 163 kg
93 divided by 70, which is about 1.3 kg
93 minus 70, which is 23 kg
70 minus 93, which is -23 kg
items.explanation: The only thing that differs between the two readings is the suitcase, so subtracting isolates it.

items.prompt: Which of these is a direct measurement?
choices: Estimating learning from a test score
Measuring a desk's width with a ruler
Judging code quality from line coverage
Inferring fitness from a daily step count
items.explanation: The ruler touches the very quantity being measured. The others read a stand-in.

items.prompt: In the chain target, proxy, instrument, number, which link is a judgment call rather than an engineering fix?
choices: How accurately the instrument reads values
How often the dashboard number is refreshed
Which unit the final number is shown in
Whether the proxy really tracks the target
items.explanation: Instrument accuracy and refresh rate can be fixed. Whether the proxy tracks the target is an assumption that needs separate evidence.

items.prompt: A team reports that support quality is up because average first-reply time fell from 9 hours to 3 hours. Which question most directly tests whether that number means what they claim?
choices: Whether the 3-hour figure was rounded to the nearest whole hour by the reporting tool
Whether the chart uses the same colors and axis labels as last quarter's report
Whether the 9-hour baseline was gathered on a different weekday than the new figure
Whether faster first replies actually track customers getting their problem solved
items.explanation: The claim depends on the link between first-reply time and support quality, the dotted link in the chain. Rounding and weekday issues are secondary instrument or sampling concerns.
items.reference:
Direct versus indirect
📏 direct: the instrument touches the target itself
🧳 indirect: combine readings you can observe
🎯 proxy: an observable stand-in for the target
🔢 a claim needs a unit and a baseline
Why: when the target cannot be observed, the number you act on is only as good as the link between it and what you really read.
items.learnMore:
Targets you cannot read

A bathroom scale cannot weigh a suitcase you cannot put on it, so you weigh yourself twice and subtract. Code quality and learning are the same kind of target: no instrument reads them, so people read a stand-in and assume it moves with the target.

Common mistake

Treating the number on the screen as the target itself, instead of asking how closely it tracks it.
items.reflection: Pick something you care about but cannot read off a dial (a team's morale, a recipe's quality). What would you actually observe in its place, and what would that stand-in miss?

items.prompt: Which of these is a checkable measurement claim?
choices: Checkout feels much snappier since the last release shipped to everyone
Median checkout latency fell from 410 ms to 330 ms, same endpoint
Latency improved by a solid forty percent across the whole site this month
The checkout page is now among our best performing pages overall
items.explanation: It names a statistic, a unit, two values and the thing measured. The others are directions or percentages with no baseline.

items.prompt: A heavy box fits on no scale, but you can weigh yourself. Which plan isolates the box, and what does it cost you?
choices: Weigh yourself holding it once, because a fixed scale offset then cancels out anyway
Weigh yourself holding it twice and average, because averaging removes all rounding doubt
Weigh yourself with and without it and subtract, accepting the added rounding doubt
Weigh yourself alone and add the box's printed size, because volume tells you weight
items.explanation: Subtraction isolates the box, but each reading carries its own rounding doubt, and the difference carries both.

items.prompt: Daily active users is used as a proxy for user happiness. Which finding most directly shows the proxy has detached from the target?
choices: Daily users rose 20% after an unskippable popup, while satisfaction fell
Daily users fluctuate by a few percent between weekdays and weekends every week
Daily users are counted by one service while the surveys come from another team
Daily users reached a new peak in the same month as a big seasonal sale
items.explanation: The proxy and the target moved in opposite directions after a change that served the number, not the people. The others are ordinary noise or coincidence.

items.prompt: What does the resolution of a display mean?
choices: The number of readings taken on each occasion
The largest value the instrument can display
The smallest step the display can show
The unit that the displayed numbers are given in
items.explanation: Resolution is the step size. A whole-kilogram scale has a resolution of 1 kg.

items.prompt: A scale shows whole kilograms and reads 70. The true value lies within which range?
choices: 69 to 71 kg
items.explanation: Rounding to the nearest whole kilogram means the true value is within half a step either way.

items.prompt: Two readings, each off by up to 0.5 kg, are subtracted. What is the largest possible error in the difference?
choices: 0 kg
0.5 kg
2 kg
1 kg
items.explanation: In the worst case one reading is 0.5 too high and the other 0.5 too low, so the errors add to 1 kg.

items.prompt: A scale always reads 2 kg too heavy. What kind of error is that?
choices: Random
Systematic
Resolution
Sampling
items.explanation: An error that is the same every time is systematic. It shifts all readings equally.

items.prompt: Your reading wobbles 69, 71, 70, 72 on the same load. Which error is this?
choices: Random error
Fixed offset
Unit mismatch
Wrong target
items.explanation: Readings that scatter around a value show random error.

items.prompt: Subtracting two readings from the same scale cancels which error?
choices: The rounding of each displayed reading
The random wobble of each reading
A constant offset shared by both readings
Doubt about whether the proxy is valid
items.explanation: A constant offset appears in both readings and drops out of the difference. Rounding and wobble do not.

items.prompt: A scale with 0.5 kg steps replaces one with 1 kg steps. What happens to each reading's range?
choices: It disappears completely
Its width is halved
Its width is doubled
It changes only for heavy items
items.explanation: Halving the step halves the range, but never removes it.

items.prompt: On a 1 kg scale the readings differ by 23 kg and the limit is 23 kg. What is the honest verdict?
choices: Within the limit, since 23 is not more than the limit of 23
Over the limit, since the range includes values up to 24
Within the limit, since the errors usually cancel out
Cannot tell; the true value could be anywhere from 22 to 24
items.explanation: The limit falls inside the 22 to 24 range, so the data neither proves nor disproves it.

items.prompt: A kitchen scale shows 5 g steps. A bowl alone reads 120 g and bowl plus flour reads 370 g. Which range holds the flour's true weight?
items.explanation: The displayed difference is 250 g and the doubt is one full step of 5 g each way. 247.5 to 252.5 forgets the second reading's doubt; 240 to 260 counts two steps.
items.reference:
Reading a rounded number
📐 resolution: the smallest step the display shows
± a reading is uncertain by half a step
➖ a difference can be off by a full step
🔁 offsets cancel in a difference, wobble does not
Why: each displayed value stands for a range, and combining readings combines their ranges.
items.learnMore:
A reading is a range

A scale that shows whole kilograms reports 70 for anything from 69.5 to 70.5. Subtract two such readings and the worst case pairs the highest first value with the lowest second one, so the doubt is a full step each way. A constant offset is the same in both readings, so subtracting removes it.

Common mistake

Treating a displayed number as exact, or assuming that subtracting readings makes their errors cancel.
items.reflection: Think of a number you rely on that is rounded (a time, a price, a weight). Where would the hidden half-step matter to a decision?

items.prompt: A scale reads 3 kg too heavy, and each reading also wobbles by up to 1 kg. Two readings are subtracted. What describes the error in the result?
choices: Both cancel, leaving only the rounding of the display itself
The 3 kg offset cancels, but the wobble can still add to 2 kg
The offset cancels and the wobble cancels as well, leaving nothing
Neither cancels, so the error can reach as much as 5 kg
items.explanation: A shared offset drops out of a difference. Independent wobble can point in opposite directions in the two readings and add up to 2 kg.

Accuracy can only ever be claimed once a thousand separate readings are collected
Repeatability describes scatter, but a systematic offset can shift every reading
A scale cannot be both repeatable and accurate at the very same time
items.explanation: Tight repeats say nothing about whether the cluster is centered on the truth.

choices: Neither settles it, but B's 22.8 to 23.2 range is five times narrower
Only B settles it, because its 0.2 step is below A's half-step of 0.5
Both settle it, since the limit equals the displayed difference on each
Only A is undecided, because B's smaller steps make its reading exact
items.explanation: A's range is 22 to 24 (width 2) and B's is 22.8 to 23.2 (width 0.4). Both still contain 23.

items.prompt: What does reliability mean for a measurement?
choices: The readings are close to the quantity you care about
The instrument has a very fine step on its display, in any unit
Repeated readings of the same thing agree with each other
The reading is shown in a standard unit
items.explanation: Reliability, or precision, is about repeatability.

items.prompt: What does validity mean for a measurement?
choices: The readings are close to what you actually care about
Repeated readings of the same thing agree closely
The instrument is cheap, light and easy for anyone to use
The number is refreshed on a regular schedule
items.explanation: Validity, or accuracy, is about measuring the right thing and getting it right.

items.prompt: A scale reads 5 lb too heavy, every single time. How would you describe it?
choices: Valid but not reliable
Both reliable and valid
Neither reliable nor valid
Reliable but not valid
items.explanation: Its readings repeat (reliable) but sit in the wrong place (not valid).

items.prompt: A sensor gives a different value each time for an unchanging quantity. What is low?
choices: Its validity
Its reliability
Its resolution
Its offset
items.explanation: Readings that scatter for the same quantity show low reliability.

items.prompt: Which reading sounds trustworthy but may hide a problem?
choices: A number that is exactly the same every day
A number that fluctuates a lot between days
A number that changed after a known fix
A number that is shown with its unit
items.explanation: Perfect stability can mean a stuck cache or a biased sample.

items.prompt: How can you check whether a suspect scale is valid?
choices: Weigh the same item ten times and compare readings
Check that the display never flickers between readings
Weigh a known 10 kg object and compare the reading
Read the manual's accuracy claim a second time
items.explanation: Validity needs an independent known value. Repeats only test reliability.

items.prompt: What does bias mean in a measurement method?
choices: The readings jump around at random
The method is tilted in one direction
The instrument shows very fine display steps
The unit is not a standard one
items.explanation: Bias is a consistent tilt, such as measuring only the fastest requests.

items.prompt: Which pairing of terms is correct?
choices: Validity goes with repeatability
Accuracy goes with the display step
Reliability goes with correctness
Precision goes with repeatability
items.explanation: Precision and reliability are about agreement between readings; accuracy and validity are about closeness to the truth.

items.prompt: A latency dashboard shows 212 ms every day for a month, to the millisecond, although real traffic is known to vary. What should you check first?
choices: Whether the service is simply so stable that no further check is needed
Whether the dashboard rounds each value to the nearest whole millisecond
Whether percentiles are naturally constant over a month of varying load
Whether the panel reads a cached or stale value instead of live data
items.explanation: Perfect stability against varying traffic is a symptom, and a stale value is the likeliest cause.
items.reference:
Two separate questions
🔁 reliability: do repeated readings agree?
🎯 validity: are they near what you care about?
⚠️ reliable but not valid: tight cluster, wrong place
🧪 check validity with an independent known value
Why: consistency feels like trustworthiness, but only a comparison with something independent can show a reading is correct.
items.learnMore:
Precision is not accuracy

A scale that reads 2 kg heavy every time never contradicts itself, which is exactly why it is easy to trust. Averaging more readings tightens the cluster but moves it nowhere; only checking against a known weight or an independent method reveals the offset.

Common mistake

Treating a stable number as an accurate number.
items.reflection: Think of a number in your life that never changes (a clock that is always 5 minutes fast, a habit tracker that always says you did well). What independent check could you make?

items.prompt: Which measurement is reliable but not valid?
choices: A p99 reading that swings between 300 and 900 ms under identical load every day
A coverage score that counts tests with no assertions, identical on every run
A calibrated scale on an unstable table that jitters by about 1 kg per reading
An average of many noisy readings that centers on the true value of the target
items.explanation: Only the first repeats exactly while measuring the wrong thing. The second is unreliable and the other two are valid.

items.prompt: A team averages 100 noisy readings from a scale that reads 2 kg too heavy. What does the averaging improve?
choices: Validity: the offset averages out together with all of the noise
Both: enough readings will fix every kind of error, not just noise
Reliability: the scatter shrinks, but the 2 kg offset stays
Neither: averaging only helps if the offset itself is random
items.explanation: Averaging reduces random scatter. A systematic offset is shared by every reading, so it survives.

items.prompt: Which check can reveal that a perfectly stable metric is invalid?
choices: Compare it with an independent measurement of the same target
Repeat the same measurement more times with the same method
Increase the display resolution of the dashboard panel
Ask the owners whether the number has ever changed
items.explanation: Only an independent comparison can expose an offset or a wrong proxy; repeating the same method reproduces the same flaw.

items.prompt: Which sentence best states Goodhart's law?
choices: Any measure improves whenever people know they are being watched closely
The most precise measure is always the best target
When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure
Two measures of the same thing always agree on average
items.explanation: Targeting a measure changes behavior in ways that break its link to what it stood for.

items.prompt: Team B added tests that assert nothing to raise coverage. What happened to the real target?
choices: It peaked and then fell while coverage kept rising
It rose steadily and in step with coverage the whole time
It stayed flat at its starting value
It fell from the first test that was added
items.explanation: In the model, Team B's real target peaks near 53 and ends at 30 while coverage reaches 100.

items.prompt: In the model, what happens to the proxy score as pressure goes from 0 to 100?
choices: It peaks near 53 and then falls
It stays at 40 for any pressure
It falls from 100 to 40
It climbs from 40 to 100
items.explanation: The proxy score is 40 plus 0.6 times the pressure, capped at 100, whatever the correlation.

items.prompt: At low pressure, how do the proxy and the real target relate?
choices: They move in opposite directions
They tend to move together
The proxy rises while the target is flat
They are unrelated from the start
items.explanation: That early agreement is why the proxy looked like a good idea.

items.prompt: Which school example matches the Goodhart pattern?
choices: Rewarding test scores only, so students memorize answer patterns
Giving every student the same textbook for the whole school year
Holding the exams in a quiet room with good natural lighting
Letting students choose the order they study their subjects in
items.explanation: The score rises while the real learning it stood for may not.

items.prompt: Why did Team A's real target keep rising under pressure?
choices: Its coverage number was lower than Team B's
Its instrument was more precise than Team B's
Its proxy's correlation with the target stayed strong
Its sample of tests was larger than Team B's
items.explanation: A strong correlation (0.9 in the model) keeps the penalty small.

items.prompt: In the model, what is Team B's real target at pressure 100?
items.explanation: With correlation 0.3 the penalty is 70, so 100 minus 70 gives 30.

items.prompt: Which is evidence that a proxy is being gamed?
choices: The number is exactly the same on each weekday, week after week
The number is shown with its unit attached next to the title
The number is measured by an automated tool, not by hand
The number climbs while independent outcomes stall or worsen
items.explanation: A rising proxy with a non-rising target is the signature of the break.

items.prompt: In the model with correlation 0.3, what are the proxy score and the real target at pressure 50?
choices: Proxy 70, real target 68
Proxy 53, real target about 70
Proxy 50, real target 50
Proxy 70, real target about 53
items.explanation: The proxy is 40 + 0.6 x 50 = 70. The real target is 70 minus 50 squared times 0.7 times 0.01, which is 70 minus 17.5, or 52.5.
items.reference:
When the stand-in becomes the goal
📈 the proxy keeps climbing under pressure
🎯 the target rises with it only while correlation holds
📉 a weak proxy peaks, then the target falls
🔍 check the target independently, not just the proxy
Why: once effort goes to the number itself, the link that made it a good stand-in is no longer protected.
items.learnMore:
Goodhart's law

A measure is chosen because it tracks something real. Reward the measure and people will find cheaper ways to raise it than improving the real thing. In the unit's model the proxy score is 40 plus 0.6 times the pressure, capped at 100, while the real target loses a penalty that grows with pressure squared and shrinks as correlation rises.

Common mistake

Believing that a proxy that was valid once stays valid after it becomes a target.
items.reflection: Think of a score someone at your school or workplace is judged by. What is the cheapest way to raise it without improving what it was meant to show?

items.prompt: Two teams show 100 coverage at pressure 100, with correlations 0.9 and 0.3. What can you conclude about their real targets?
choices: They are equal, since the proxy score is identical
Nothing without the correlation; the model gives 90 and 30
The lower-correlation team is higher, since it worked harder
Both exceed 90, since coverage sits at its cap
items.explanation: The proxy score never depends on correlation, so identical proxies can hide very different real outcomes.

Publish it more widely so everyone sees the same number
items.explanation: Becoming a target is exactly when a proxy is most likely to detach, so its link needs fresh evidence.

🎯 the target rises with it only while correlation holds
📉 a weak proxy peaks, then the target falls
🔍 check the target independently, not just the proxy
Why: once effort goes to the number itself, the link that made it a good stand-in is no longer protected.
items.learnMore:
Goodhart's law

A measure is chosen because it tracks something real. Reward the measure and people will find cheaper ways to raise it than improving the real thing. In the unit's model the proxy score is 40 plus 0.6 times the pressure, capped at 100, while the real target loses a penalty that grows with pressure squared and shrinks as correlation rises.

Common mistake

Believing that a proxy that was valid once stays valid after it becomes a target.

items.prompt: What is sampling?
choices: Measuring the whole thing twice and averaging the readings
Rounding a reading to the nearest step
Measuring a part in order to learn about the whole
Replacing a target with a stand-in
items.explanation: Sampling infers the whole from a subset, which adds its own error.

items.prompt: You ask four times as many random people. What happens to sampling error?
choices: It is roughly cut in half
It is roughly cut to a quarter
It stays about the same size
It roughly doubles in size
items.explanation: Error shrinks with the square root of n, and the square root of 4 is 2.

items.prompt: A random sample goes from n = 100 to n = 400. By what factor does the typical error change?
choices: It is divided by 4
It is multiplied by 2
It is multiplied by 4
It is divided by 2
items.explanation: 400 is four times 100, and sqrt(4) = 2.

items.prompt: Going from a 1% sample to a 4% sample of traffic changes the error by what factor?
choices: It is quartered
It is halved
It is doubled
It is unchanged
items.explanation: A 4 times larger random sample halves the error.

items.prompt: Doubling a random sample size lowers the error by about what percent?
items.explanation: The error is divided by sqrt(2), about 1.41, which is a reduction of about 29%.

items.prompt: Which sample best represents all students for a lunch survey?
choices: Students standing in line at the lunch queue today
Friends of the person doing the survey
Names drawn at random from the full school roll
Students who chose to fill in a form
items.explanation: Random selection from everyone avoids a built-in tilt.

items.prompt: What does standard error describe?
choices: The rounding of the instrument's display
Chance variation from sampling, not bias
A constant offset in every reading
The cost of collecting the sample
items.explanation: It measures how much random samples differ from each other, nothing about a bad sampling method.

items.prompt: For a 50/50 yes-no share, what is the typical error at n = 40?
choices: About 15.8 percentage points
About 4.0 percentage points
About 2.0 percentage points
About 7.9 percentage points
items.explanation: 0.5 divided by the square root of 40 is about 0.079.

items.prompt: For a 50/50 yes-no share, the error at n = 40 is about 7.9 points. What is it at n = 160?
choices: About 2.0 points
About 5.9 points
About 7.9 points
About 4.0 points
items.explanation: 160 is 4 times 40, so the error halves: 7.9 / 2 is about 4.0. The 2.0 belongs to n = 640.
items.reference:
How much a sample can tell you
🎲 random sample: error shrinks as 1 / sqrt(n)
4️⃣ four times the sample halves the error
📊 50/50 share: 15.8, 7.9, 4.0, 2.0 points
🧲 a biased sample converges on the wrong value
Why: standard error describes chance variation only, so a larger sample cannot fix a sample that was chosen badly.
items.learnMore:
Diminishing returns and bias

For a random sample the typical error is spread divided by the square root of n. That is why each 4 times more data only halves it, and why dropping sampling entirely buys little. None of this applies if the sample is not random: asking only the lunch queue converges precisely on the queue's opinion.

Common mistake

Expecting twice the sample to halve the error, or trusting a large sample that was never random.

items.prompt: Implement `halfStep(step)` that returns half of the display step. For a 1 kg scale that is 0.5.
items.explanation: A rounded reading is uncertain by half a step each way, so the half-step is the basic unit of doubt.

items.prompt: Implement `readingRange(reading, step)` that returns `[low, high]`, the range a displayed reading can stand for.
items.explanation: The true value is within half a step below and above the displayed value.

items.prompt: Implement `rangeWidth(range)` that takes `[low, high]` and returns how wide the range is.
items.explanation: The width is the high end minus the low end, and it measures how much doubt remains.

items.prompt: Implement `isUnder(range, limit)` that returns true only when the whole `[low, high]` range is at or below the limit.
items.explanation: To be certain the value is under the limit, even its highest possible value must be at or below it.

items.prompt: Implement `differenceOfReadings(a, b)` that returns the displayed difference `a - b` between two readings.
items.explanation: The displayed difference is the plain subtraction; the doubt around it is a separate step.

items.prompt: Implement `isUndecided(range, limit)` that returns true when the limit falls strictly inside `[low, high]`, so the data cannot decide.
items.explanation: If the limit is below the low end or above the high end the data decides; strictly between them it cannot.

items.prompt: Implement `diffRange(withReading, withoutReading, step)` that returns `[low, high]` for the true difference of two readings that each have the given display step.
items.explanation: Each reading is off by up to half a step, and in the worst case the errors point opposite ways, so the difference is off by a full step either way.
items.reference:
Bounds on a combined reading
📐 one reading: ± half a step
➖ a difference: ± a full step
➕ a sum of n readings: ± n half-steps
🚦 compare the range to the limit: within, over, or unknown
Why: the worst case pairs every reading's error in the same direction, so the doubt is the sum of the half-steps.
items.learnMore:
Worst-case bounds

A displayed value stands for a range of half a step each way. For a difference the worst case is first high, second low (and the reverse), so the range is the displayed difference minus and plus one full step. If the limit falls inside the range, the data cannot decide.

Common mistake

Using only a half-step for a difference, or answering within or over when the limit sits inside the range.
items.reflection: Take a calculation you do with rounded numbers (a budget, a recipe). Which total is the most uncertain, and does the answer ever hinge on it?

items.explanation: Compute the worst-case range first, then compare both ends with the limit. Only when the whole range is on one side is the verdict certain. When the low end merely equals the limit the true value could still be exactly at it, so it stays unknown.
